title: The Cloth Mother and the Wire Mother
text:
In the 1950s, at the University of Wisconsin, the psychologist Harry Harlow raised infant rhesus monkeys away from their mothers. In each cage he placed two artificial mothers. One was a bare cylinder of wire mesh with a carved face. The other had the same shape but was wrapped in soft terry cloth. For some babies only the wire mother held a bottle of milk; for others only the cloth one did.

The prevailing theory of the time said that an infant loves its mother because she feeds it. Harlow's monkeys disagreed. Even when all their milk came from the wire figure, they went to it only to drink and then hurried back to the cloth mother, spending most of the day clinging to her.

When Harlow frightened them with a clanking mechanical toy, the babies ran to the cloth mother, held on, and soon calmed down enough to look at the strange object and even explore it. Placed in an unfamiliar room with the cloth mother present, they used her as a safe base. Without her, they froze, cried and huddled in a corner.

Harlow reported these results in 1958 under the title "The Nature of Love." They helped overturn the idea that a child's attachment is only about food and supported the view that touch and comfort are needs in their own right.
lesson: Feeding, housing and providing are not enough. Children need warmth, touch and a safe person to run back to before they dare to explore.
source: Harlow, H. F. (1958). The nature of love. American Psychologist, 13(12), 673-685.
caveat: The experiments caused severe distress to the animals and are now widely cited as an example of research that would not be permitted today.
